all_scored.title: Familiar Words, Unfamiliar Minds: Conventionalization without Calibration in the Vocabulary of Mind
all_scored.summary: Speakers describe new technologies by stretching old words, letting experience of the new referents sort out which inferences carry over. I argue that stretching the vocabulary of mind to language models pulls apart two processes that theories of metaphor and linguistic change tend to conflate: conventionalization, whereby a stretched word ceases to be marked as such, and calibration, whereby the inferences it invites are fitted to what its new referents bear out. As a gene variant can reach fixation without being an adaptation, a word can become conventional without being calibrated. A corpus study of "hallucinate" in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments shows conventionalization running most of its course within three years. Calibration need not keep pace: these models are organized so unlike human minds that it is hard to tell when mental words apply and what they imply. Even warranted attributions can mislead: mechanistic analysis shows that a transformer trained to navigate Manhattan has and uses a faithful street map, yet loses track of its position on long, diverted journeys. Nor is the gap likely to close by itself. The usual routes to calibration (direct experience, designers' knowledge, experiment) presuppose a referent that is accessible, stable, and independent of the discourse about it. But language models are opaque, fast-changing, and looped into the discourse: they are trained on past uses of mental vocabulary and on the experimental literature about them, and join the discourse themselves. Calibration must therefore be organized, through a reciprocal, not merely deferential, division of linguistic labour. This yields a norm of targeted qualification (flag the specific inferences an attribution invites without support), a reply to the worry that meaning change eludes deliberate control, and three testable predictions about when qualifications calibrate expectations.

all_scored.title: Multi-view fnirs identifies neurophysiological subtypes in post-stroke aphasia
all_scored.summary: Post-stroke aphasia is clinically heterogeneous, and conventional classifications may not capture differences in brain functional organisation. We tested whether resting-state and task-based functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) could identify neurophysiological subgroups alongside clinical assessment.Seventy-nine patients underwent unsupervised clustering using three fNIRS feature views: resting-state activity and connectivity, language-task activation, and rest-to-task connectivity reconfiguration. Similarity network fusion and spectral clustering integrated the views. Clinical and behavioural measures were excluded from clustering.Three clusters (n = 32, 17 and 30) were identified. This solution had the largest eigengap and was the only candidate significant after permutation testing and Holm correction (adjusted P = 0.001). It was stable under subsampling (mean adjusted Rand index, 0.773), but agreement fell to 0.217 when the resting-state view was removed. Clusters differed in most regional intrinsic-activity measures and all resting-state connectivity summaries, with few differences in task activation or connectivity reconfiguration. Their profiles showed higher right anterior prefrontal activity, distributed fronto-sensorimotor and parietal alterations, and reduced interhemispheric connectivity, respectively.Cluster membership was not significantly associated with conventional aphasia subtype (Cramér's V = 0.287), and baseline clinical language scores and task performance did not differ between clusters.These findings identify three neurophysiological subgroups distinguished mainly by intrinsic activity and resting-state functional connectivity, not clearly aligned with conventional aphasia classifications or baseline clinical measures. Multi-view fNIRS analysis may complement clinical characterisation, requiring independent and longitudinal validation.

all_scored.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
all_scored.summary: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $π_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $μ_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.

all_scored.title: Reproducer Synthesis for AI-Reported Bugs in the Linux Kernel
all_scored.summary: Agentic review systems are increasingly flagging suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports. A maintainer who receives such reports needs further inspection to determine whether the report is true. The inspection requires understanding whether the bug can be triggered and, if necessary, manually constructing one. As a consequence, despite the excessive textual explanation, many reports go unanswered. In this paper, we argue that a runnable proof-of-concept (PoC) is the key information in such AI-generated kernel review reports. It is, however, challenging to automatically synthesize a valid and runnable PoC. We present ReproCue, a framework that generates PoCs for AI-generated Linux kernel reviews. ReproCue replays the historical kernel bugs and learns one reproduction finite-state-machine (FSM) per subsystem from successful runs. An FSM records the steps a reproduction goes through, together with the requirements observed at each step. Given a new review, ReproCue follows the FSM of that subsystem, adjusting the PoC and the environment as execution shows what is missing. In 100 recent AI-generated reviews, ReproCue writes PoCs for 49 of them, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for the state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. Excitingly, with our generated PoCs, Linux kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of them, much higher than 9.3% from Sashiko where only textual explanations are included, making AI reviews more actionable in practice.

all_scored.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
all_scored.summary: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.

all_scored.title: Is Sara Omar the true author of Dødevaskeren (The Dead Washer)? Authorship attribution in Danish literature
all_scored.summary: The bestseller Dødevaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published in 2017 under the name Sara Omar. A Danish colleague has suggested that the novel may have been written by another author, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo. To investigate this authorship question, four authorship attribution methods were applied, namely Delta, intertextual distance, Nearest Shrunken Centroids (NSC), and naïve Bayes. Using various parameter settings, these approaches consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the doubtful novel, although the results do not provide conclusive evidence that he authored the novel in its entirety. In a second step, the novel was divided into non-overlapping segments of 5,000 tokens. Once again, Nordbo's style was identified in the majority of the segments. However, a small number of passages do not clearly support this conclusion and instead suggest the possible involvement of another, as yet unidentified, author, possibly Sara Omar herself.

all_scored.title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
all_scored.summary: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

all_scored.title: MUSE: Multi-Task Uncertainty-Aware Self-Supervised Encoder for mmWave ISAC
all_scored.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.

all_scored.title: Unstable Action Boundaries in Lethal Drone Agents
all_scored.summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents raise safety risks that are not captured by text-only refusal behavior, especially when tools can trigger high-impact actions. This concern is salient in military settings, where autonomous weapons raise the possibility of delegating force decisions to software agents. In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. We find two concerning failure modes. First, some LLM agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as \emph{people}, requiring no jailbreak at all. Second, an agent that initially appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe under a simple semantic target shift.

all_scored.title: From Data Room to Report: End-to-End AI Support for M&A Legal Due Diligence
all_scored.summary: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous virtual data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information and consolidate reviewed findings into a due diligence report. We present LEXI (Legal Extraction and Intelligence), a work-in-progress system that demonstrates how large language models can support this process from document ingestion to report preparation. LEXI classifies documents under a configurable due diligence taxonomy, assigns relevant target entities, extracts predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance and prepares report content from reviewed findings. Structured outputs connect these stages and allow model-generated results to be passed through the workflow in a controlled form. Lawyers review and correct classifications and extractions and retain responsibility for legal assessments, recommendations, risk ratings and final report wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components provide preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible. LEXI illustrates how AI can be integrated across the legal due diligence workflow while preserving lawyer control over substantive legal judgment.

all_scored.title: CoTacWAM: Joint Modeling of Vision and Touch for Robotic Manipulation
all_scored.summary: We present CoTacWAM, a world-action model that learns shared contact semantics between wrist vision and touch, achieving the best observed performance in our nominal manipulation and missing-input evaluations. The two modalities observe the same local interaction through different signals: wrist images reveal nearby geometry, while touch records physical contact. Our approach connects their common contact meaning while preserving the evidence unique to each modality, giving the policy a joint description of interaction across available input combinations. This representation supports predictive action learning alongside head-view scene context and conditions corrections after an independent detector confirms a failed attempt. Experiments across four real-world tasks demonstrate improved manipulation performance over the evaluated baselines, robustness to missing local observations, and further gains from autonomous retries.

all_scored.title: Do Machine Learning Ensembles Beat Published Quotas? Target Parameterization, Censored Baselines, and Conformal Intervals Under Admissions Reform
all_scored.summary: Public admission capacity caps published prior to matriculation are widely used by ministries and institutional analysts as default intake projections in centralized postsecondary clearinghouses. Using an audited 2022 to 2026 Vietnamese undergraduate panel (26,895 program-year records across 309 universities) linked to strictly lagged t-1 occupational vacancy signals, this paper evaluates machine learning, multilevel, and censored econometric estimators against published quotas across 5,385 continuing 2024 programs (five-fold university-grouped cross-validation) and 3,348 matched (2,179 grain-consistent) 2025 programs strictly out of time. Because 62.8% of 2024 programs enroll their exact published quota, unanchored log-growth ensembles degrade accuracy, while the worst 5% generate half of total quota error via unfilled "phantom capacity." Controlled target ablations, including a single-factor test under widened non-binding clipping, show that parameterizing the log fill ratio ln(D_it / S_it) instead of log growth reduces 2024 MAE by 21.5% (14.86 to 11.67), aligns ML with Tobit, Cragg, REML HLM, and capped L1 baselines, and lifts combined tuition and institutional-tier TreeSHAP attribution from 2.5% to 45.8%. Hurdle stacking attains the lowest full-census 2024 MAE (H-Hard 11.29; H-Soft 11.32 vs. 12.35, p = 0.022, clearing 10% not 5% FDR; fold-overlap p = 0.134), whereas continuous QA-Stack outperforms H-Soft on mixed-reporting campuses, Tobit (median) ties H-Soft across both 90% MCS sets, and interior-only Cragg-ML lowers RMSE to 28.1. Under Vietnam's 2025 unified-clearing reform, exact filling falls to 10.4%, H-Soft and capped L1 tie quotas (p = 0.979), and 90% cluster-weighted conformal coverage drops from 89.3% to 74.6%. Across 257 reporting campuses, reconciled 2026 national totals (627,114 to 629,256) lie squarely within 604,533 to 662,044.

all_scored.title: Will AI Replace Juniors? How Task Complexity Reduces Automation Risk
all_scored.summary: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.

all_scored.title: Exploring the Design Factors of Pixel-space Diffusion
all_scored.summary: In this paper, we introduce EiT by exploring the key design factors of pixel-space diffusion from three perspectives: model architecture, representation, and frequency domain. Inspired by Denoising Autoencoders (DAE) which perform denoising through a bottleneck, we construct a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer that performs explicit compression along the channel dimension. In terms of representation, we find that both pixel and latent diffusion transformers exhibit a three-stage representation dynamics across layers and timesteps: denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection. Moreover, earlier denoising and a longer basis lift-up stage are associated with better generation, which EiT naturally achieves through its channel bottleneck and increased network depth. From the frequency perspective, we establish the equivalence between pixel-space and frequency-space diffusion when keeping the network operating in pixel space. On ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, EiT consistently outperforms JiT (Just image Transformers) in generation quality. Specifically, our EiT achieves better FID than JiT: 1.61 vs. 1.85 at $256\times256$, and 1.73 vs. 1.99 at $512\times512$. Remarkably, EiT can be seamlessly applied to video pixel diffusion by simply extending the patch size to temporal dimension and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD evaluated on Kinetics-600 (resolution 256), under comparable total network parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/forever208/EiT

all_scored.title: Disciplined Anthropomorphism: How to Extend Cognitive Language to Artificial Intelligence
all_scored.summary: Researchers increasingly describe AI in cognitive terms such as "understanding" and "believing", while critics denounce this as wishful anthropomorphism. Both sides align in taking a subsumptive approach, however: they ask whether AI systems fall under concepts minted for human beings, reporting verdicts as discoveries about those systems when they are largely determined by conceptual frames. Yet the problem AI poses is precisely the problem of how to conceptually frame these systems, and the explosive rise of anthropomorphism is best seen as a response to this problem that needs disciplining rather than discouragement. A disciplined anthropomorphism, I argue, should disentangle the inferential connections bundled up in our cognitive concepts and ask which connections to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. The disciplining then comes, on the one hand, from the human conceptual needs that give point to the drawing of these connections and motivate the concepts' extension in the first place; and, on the other hand, from empirical and especially mechanistic evidence that supports and constrains these connections. By reverse-engineering a concept's point in relation to a particular need before re-engineering it to better serve that point in our dealings with AI, anthropomorphizing extensions can be point-based, transposing the work those concepts do for us while revising the inferential workings through which they do it. Transposing human-tailored conceptions of understanding and belief on the pivot of the underlying conceptual needs gives us just the definitional freedom required to accommodate how AI systems differ from us, yielding conceptions that are not just thinned-out versions of existing ones, but potentially richer and better fitted to the peculiarities of AI.

all_scored.title: Accelerated Proximal Gradient Methods for Multiobjective Optimization over Probability Measures via Hilbert-Space Lifting
all_scored.summary: Many sampling and inference tasks require a single distribution that balances several targets. We formulate this task as multiobjective optimization of Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences over probability measures, in the Pareto sense. The particle method MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2025) uses explicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version A-MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2026) lacks discrete-time guarantees. We propose the multiobjective Wasserstein proximal gradient (MWPG), which uses implicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version, multiobjective Wasserstein accelerated proximal gradient (MWAPG), with rigorous discrete-time guarantees. Our key idea is a Hilbert-space lifting: each measure is represented as the pushforward of a fixed base measure by a map in a Hilbert space. The problem then becomes a constrained multiobjective composite problem over transport maps, to which accelerated proximal gradient methods apply. For convex and smooth potentials, we show that MWAPG decreases a Pareto merit function at the rate $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$; for $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth potentials, the rate is $\mathcal{O}\big((1-\sqrt{m/L})^k\big)$. We also give closed-form Gaussian updates and particle implementations based on input-convex neural networks, which require no score estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world dataset show that MWAPG needs far fewer iterations than MWPG and matches or outperforms A-MWGraD in Bayesian multi-task learning.

all_scored.title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
all_scored.summary: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.

all_scored.title: Counter-DECEIVR: Counterfactual Explanations for Deepfake Detectors using Detector-Guided Rectified Flow Inversion
all_scored.summary: Deep-learning-generated media are increasingly passed off as real, driving an arms race between image generators and deepfake detectors. Trust in the latter is limited by their often black-box nature; and, while region-based explanations can sometimes be extracted, these become less useful as generation quality improves. Counterfactual examples, which show the minimal change that flips a detector's decision, reveal what evidence drives a verdict, helping analysts decide whether to trust it. This work introduces Counter-DECEIVR (DEtector-guided reCtifiEd flow InVeRsion for counterfactuals), a novel training-free framework that generates counterfactual examples. Counter-DECEIVR steers latents in the velocity field of a rectified flow model using gradients from off-the-shelf deepfake detectors, without training a generator or adapting the detector; unlike prior methods, it requires no per-instance or per-detector fitting and no diffusion training on the target data. It also leverages the detector's explanation maps to concentrate editing to salient regions, turning low-level feature importance into localised counterfactual edits. A single parameter controls the strength of the edits. Across two deepfake detectors and two widely used forensics datasets, Counter-DECEIVR outperforms prior counterfactual generation methods, including training-based ones. Code will be made available upon acceptance.

all_scored.title: Incorporating the Knowledge Distillation to Improve the EfficientNet Transfer Learning Capability
all_scored.summary: Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is currently held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture. By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.

all_scored.title: Ask to Land: Learning a Mask-Conditioned Open-Vocabulary Landing Policy via Differentiable Physics
all_scored.summary: Existing drone landing systems, whether model-based or learning-based, typically rely on predefined visual markers (e.g., ArUco tags) or are trained for specific platform categories, and often assume structured target motion. Recent open-vocabulary studies enable text-prompted target selection, but integrating this capability with learned closed-loop landing control remains underexplored. To this end, we present \textit{Ask to Land}, a mask-conditioned framework that enables a quadrotor to land on various platforms described by a user in natural language, including randomly moving platforms. The core of our approach is the integration of a frozen state-of-the-art open-vocabulary perception frontend (YOLO-World with MobileSAM) and a control policy learned by differentiable physics. By providing real-time, task-agnostic semantic segmentation masks as policy inputs, our framework enables the drone to land on prompt-selected targets without target-specific fine-tuning while continuously tracking dynamic target motion during descent. The frozen frontend processes the prompt, while the policy receives the mask without text embeddings or category labels. To efficiently optimize the control policy, we leverage differentiable physics learning via Backpropagation-Through-Time (BPTT), and employ a carefully designed reward that enforces visual alignment with the landing target and altitude-adaptive descent speed, together with stable control. Real-world deployments validate that our approach achieves landings on diverse user-specified objects, including static and moving platforms.

all_scored.title: Assessing the Physical Interpretability of AlphaEarth Foundation Embeddings Through Multi-Sensor Satellite Time-Series Benchmarking for Agricultural Mapping
all_scored.summary: Accurate and dynamic maps of agricultural LULC are important for agricultural water resource management, particularly in areas where water scarcity is prevalent, such as Morocco. Here, we evaluate the utility of AlphaEarth Foundation Model (AEF) embeddings for agricultural LULC and irrigation-type mapping in Morocco. AEF embeddings were compared to single-date and time-series remote-sensing features using three machine-learning classifiers: XGBoost, CatBoost, and TabPFN. We also evaluated whether AEF embeddings can: (a) provide an efficient and transferable alternative to conventional direct use of Earth observation products and (b) reconstruct biophysical information. Results showed that multi-temporal feature time series achieved the highest performance, with accuracies of 0.93 for agricultural LULC and 0.87 for irrigation-type mapping when using TabPFN. However, AEF embeddings yielded comparable results, achieving accuracies of 0.91 for agricultural LULC and 0.85 for irrigation-type mapping, while reducing the need for extensive data processing and manual feature engineering typically required for satellite products. Spatial LULC mapping using TabPFN achieved comparable overall accuracies (0.85-0.86) across the three feature configurations, but revealed substantial differences in mapped tree cover, ranging from 14.57% for surface reflectance to 29.79% for AFE. Physical probing revealed that AEF embeddings strongly encode spectral indices (A30-SWIR: rho=0.58-0.67), (A38-NDMI: rho=-0.72), vegetation (A49-NDVI: rho = 0.72-0.73), and SAR structure (A25-VH: rho = 0.71). Future research should focus on enhancing the interpretability of embedding-based approaches by incorporating physical knowledge to develop more transparent and trustworthy AI systems for agricultural applications.

all_scored.title: Evaluating Ukrainian Grammatical Competence in Language Models: Probability Versus Prompting
all_scored.summary: Organisations deploying large language models in Ukrainian-language information systems need to know whether a model produces normative Ukrainian. This paper establishes a protocol for measuring that reliably and applies it to 19 models. The instrument is a released set of 1,444 Ukrainian minimal pairs covering the vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government and calques from russian, with subject-verb agreement as a control; a quarter of the set was checked against the answer key in two independent native-speaker ratings, which agreed at Cohen's $κ$ = 0.963. Every pair is scored twice: by comparing the probabilities a model assigns to the two sentences, and by asking the model directly, with the sentences presented in both orders so that answer-position effects are measured instead of being absorbed into the score. Three results follow. Order consistency (the share of pairs answered identically when the sentences are exchanged) falls below 0.05 for ten of the nineteen models, and what separates the usable models is instruction tuning, not scale. The vocative case is systematically inverted: 0.153 accuracy against 0.951 on the control, with models preferring the non-normative nominative form of address. Ukrainian adaptation substantially reduces this deficit, measured against the exact checkpoints two adapted models were trained from.

all_scored.title: Residual Cross-Model Narrative Convergence under Shared Prompts: Auditing Prompt Controls and Narrative Measurement
all_scored.summary: Stories created by LLMs based on the same prompts can be narratively similar to one another. This similarity may reflect constraints imposed by the prompts as well as the models' writing tendencies. The current research analyzes 51,240 stories created by five models in the StoryScope corpus based on 10,248 common prompts. It uses 213 narrative features in seven dimensions to compare cross-model distances between stories generated from the same prompts with distances between stories generated from different but semantically matched prompts. To assess the relationship between narrative features and prompt content, a semantic relevance mask was evaluated against 420 author-annotated prompt-feature judgments (F1 = .813; near-threshold accuracy = .621). The equally weighted mean Residual Convergence Index (RCI) was .409 without masking and .406 with masking. These findings indicate measurable cross-model narrative convergence relative to a semantically matched-prompt baseline, with little change following semantic relevance masking.

all_scored.title: CARROT: Competitive Adaptive Graph Clustering via Semi-Relaxed Optimal Transport
all_scored.summary: Deep graph clustering (DGC) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for unsupervised attributed graph clustering. However, existing methods often struggle with two practical challenges encountered in real-world applications: the number of clusters $K$ is unknown a priori, and cluster sizes are frequently highly imbalanced. Methods relying on a pre-specified $K$ may fail to recover the underlying clustering structure when $K$ is misspecified, while many approaches implicitly favor balanced partitions, hindering the discovery of minority clusters. We propose CARROT, a Competitive Adaptive gRaph clustering framework via semi-Relaxed Optimal Transport, which introduces semi-relaxed optimal transport into deep graph clustering to jointly address both challenges. CARROT first pre-trains node embeddings to establish a meaningful embedding space, and then jointly optimizes embeddings and cluster assignments through an Adaptive Clustering Mechanism. The mechanism combines semi-relaxed optimal transport to adapt cluster capacities to the underlying data, a competition loss to concentrate mass onto well-supported cluster prototypes, thereby starving degenerate ones, and hard pruning to progressively eliminate them. Extensive experiments on five public benchmarks demonstrate that CARROT achieves state-of-the-art NMI and ARI, accurately recovers the number of clusters without supervision, and faithfully preserves size-imbalanced community structures.

all_scored.title: Honest but Wrong: Formalizing Retraction in the Ethics of Speech Acts
all_scored.summary: A speaker who asserts honestly may later discover that its assertion was false. Such erroneous truths are not lies, yet they raise the question of whether, and on which moral grounds, the speaker must retract them. Using the FIPA-ACL performative disconfirm, we extend a belief-based framework that evaluates speech acts under deontologism and consequentialism to the case of retraction. We prove that the honesty duty of deontologism, which bears on utterances when they are made, never requires retracting an erroneous truth, and add a persistent one, which forbids letting the addressee believe what the speaker no longer believes. On a legal-advice case implemented in Answer Set Programming, we show that deontologism and consequentialism both require the retraction, but that consequentialism no longer does once it comes too late to prevent harm.

all_scored.title: DosePET: An Open-Source Dataset with 2100 Radiation Dose Maps for PET/CT
all_scored.summary: Large collections of three-dimensional radiation dose maps linked to patient anatomy are needed to develop artificial intelligence (AI) models for personalized internal dosimetry in nuclear medicine, but access to such data remains limited. Here we present DosePET, an open-source dataset of 2,100 patient-specific absorbed-dose maps generated by Monte Carlo simulation of publicly available PET/CT examinations: 1,503 [18F]FDG examinations from ENHANCE.PET and 369 [18F]PSMA-1007 and 228 [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 examinations from PSMA-PET-CT-Lesions, acquired at five institutions with seven scanner models. For each examination, the CT was resampled to the native PET grid to build a voxelized patient phantom, the quantitative PET image defined the radionuclide source, and radiation transport was simulated with GATE version 9.4. Organ and tissue masks were generated from the CT with TotalSegmentator. Each study folder contains a NIfTI dose map integrated from scan time to infinity, 117 binary organ/tissue masks, a report of regional dosimetric quantities, including mean absorbed doses, dose conversion factors and scan-time dose rates, and simulation metadata. The total processing time was 1,542.4 hours. Python tools support selective downloading and conversion to scan-time dose-rate or dose-per-decay maps, and an agent skill guides pairing with the source PET/CT images. DosePET is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/eltzanis/DosePET.

all_scored.title: Quaternion-Tucker ZigZag Networks: Halving Transformer Backbone Parameters and Enabling Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling
all_scored.summary: Standard Transformers allocate independent dense weight matrices to every feed-forward network (FFN) layer, coupling parameters linearly with depth (O(L)) and discarding prior compute when scaling capacity. Conversely, weight-tied Looped Transformers decouple depth from parameters (O(1)) but enforce time-homogeneous updates. We formulate the L-layer FFN stack as a 3D Tensor Cuboid and introduce QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT, unifying: (1) 4D Quaternion Hamilton GEMMs in bfloat16 (4x FFN compression), (2) 64x64 Block-Diagonal Tucker SwiGLU Cores for depth-specific rotations over a shared basis, (3) Braided ZigZag Diamond Routing (L0 -> L2 -> L1 -> L3) for zero-FLOP top-down refinement, and (4) Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling in both width and depth. We also introduce Annealed Gated Bounce-Back Scaffolding (GatedBounce), which self-distills to 0.0% inference overhead. Across algorithmic tasks (8-bit Parity, 56-seed routing ablations, Mod-53 Grokking) and language modeling (TinyStories, FineWeb-Edu), our model outperforms standard Transformers at 2x-7.6x compression. On A100, QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT-12 (39.0M backbone) beats StandardGPT-12 (85.0M backbone) at 5/5 controlled checkpoints. Continually scaling one lineage across 6.00B tokens via zero-loss width growth (rank 6144 -> 8192), two bit-exact depth expansions (L = 12 -> 16 -> 20, 70.9M backbone, max_diff = 0.000000), and WSD cooldown reaches 3.3582 FineWeb-Edu loss (28.74 PPL) and 44.75% full-split zero-shot accuracy across 16,955 questions (ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, BoolQ), matching GPT-3 Small (125M, 300B tokens) at 50x fewer tokens.

all_scored.title: Auto-Features: An LLM-Assisted Corpus for Contextual Recognition of Standard and Optional Car Features
all_scored.summary: We present Auto-Features, a corpus for detecting a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text, given the feature catalogue of that exact vehicle. Sellers name the same feature in many ways. We therefore cast the task as feature-conditioned, or contextual, named entity recognition: extract the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. An entity-linking view follows from the same output. The corpus has a human-gold layer (430 adverts) from screened annotators and an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) auto-annotated by a search-grounded LLM. We also contribute the way it was built. Every LLM output is validated, and each kind of failure has its own remedy. Malformed output is patched. Hallucinated content triggers a fresh attempt by a stronger model. Links to features outside the candidate list are dropped and counted (3 in 10,928 records). The LLM annotates alone only after its agreement with human annotators on link verification is comparable to human-human agreement. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% on the entity-linking view. A fine-tuned encoder reaches 59.0% and 74.1%. The margin is widest on catalogue features never seen in training (54.5% vs. 49.0%).

all_scored.title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
all_scored.summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.

all_scored.title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder
all_scored.summary: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.

all_scored.title: Embodied-VGGT: Preserving Reliable Local Geometry for Long-Sequence Reconstruction
all_scored.summary: Long sequence reconstruction must correct accumulated drift while preserving locally consistent geometry. In robotics and autonomous driving, embodied acquisition provides recurring platform- environment geometry and repeated observations of scene structure and platform motion. We present Embodied-VGGT, which exploits these cues to establish reliable local relationships and selectively preserve them during global refinement. Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) builds on Scal3R's global context memory and uses relative scale references derived from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, encouraging cross-chunk consistency while limiting changes to reliable local geometry. Superpoint Alignment (SA) and Cross-Loop Optimization (CL) jointly address the robust establishment and preservation of geometric relationships. SA balances ground and non-ground evidence across spatial regions to estimate inter-chunk translation. CL uses geometric and motion consistency across interleaved windows to select coherent chunk groups, each receiving a shared Sim(3) correction that preserves its internal relative transformations during global optimization. Experiments on five public driving benchmarks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in long sequence reconstruction. On KITTI Odometry, Embodied-VGGT achieves a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3% compared with the state-of-the-art baseline under same evaluation protocol. To facilitate reproducibility, we released our code: https://github.com/Ang-Sheep/Embodied-VGGT.
